name: SARS & Tax Refund Scams
summary: Emails and SMSes impersonating SARS offer a refund or threaten an audit, to capture eFiling credentials or banking details.

typicalLoss.note: Control of an eFiling profile allows a criminal to redirect legitimate refunds and to file fraudulent returns in your name.

howItWorks.detail: Volume spikes during filing season when a message from SARS is entirely expected and a refund is plausible.
Two scripts dominate: a refund of a specific, believable amount awaiting your banking details, or a notice of audit and penalties requiring immediate login.
The link opens a copy of the eFiling portal. Your username, password and OTP are relayed to a criminal logging into the real portal at the same moment.
Inside the profile, banking details and the registered contact address are changed, so future correspondence and refunds go to them.
In some cases a return is filed with inflated deductions to generate a large refund into the fraudster's account, leaving you facing the assessment and penalties.

redFlags: An email or SMS with a link to log into eFiling. Always navigate to the site yourself instead.
A refund amount quoted before you have submitted or been assessed.
Threats of immediate arrest, penalty or account freezing. SARS follows formal, documented processes.
The sender domain is not the official SARS domain, or uses a lookalike with extra words.
An attachment claiming to be a statement of account or audit letter that you did not request.
illustrativeCase: During filing season a consultant receives an email formatted exactly like a SARS notice stating a R14 217.63 refund is ready pending bank verification. He logs in through the link. Nothing appears to happen, so he closes it. Two weeks later his real refund of R14 217 is paid into an account he does not recognise, and his profile's contact email has been changed.
howToProtect: Never log into eFiling from a link. Type the address yourself or use the official app, every time.
Set up and check your eFiling profile's registered banking and contact details periodically.
Treat urgency and threats as evidence of fraud rather than of officialdom.
Use a unique password for eFiling and enable every available security feature.
Verify anything unexpected by phoning SARS on their published contact number.
ifYouveBeenHit: Log into eFiling directly and change your password immediately.
Check and correct your banking details, contact email and cellphone number on the profile.
Report the incident to SARS through their official fraud reporting channel.
Open a SAPS case if a refund was diverted.
Ask your tax practitioner to review recent submissions for returns you did not file.

faqs.q: Does SARS ever email about refunds?
faqs.a: SARS does send notifications, but genuine ones direct you to log in yourself rather than through an embedded login link, and they never ask for banking details by email or SMS.

faqs.q: Someone filed a return in my name. Am I liable?
faqs.a: You must report it to SARS immediately and formally. Assessments arising from fraudulent submissions can be disputed, but only if you raise it rather than ignore the correspondence.

faqs.q: I clicked but did not enter anything. Am I fine?
faqs.a: Probably, but change your eFiling password anyway and check your registered details. It costs five minutes.
